title: Supplement to the fourth, fifth and sixth editions of the Encyclopaedia Britannica - Volume 4 - EB.13
text: Though the expense of lighting by gas from oil appears, on a large scale, not to be much less than double that of coal gas, the same great dispropier will not altogether hold for very limited quantities of light where the charge for an unrelated forms a considerable part of the current expenditure. A cool gas apparatus, however small, will, when in work, require the name, constant attention of a person to manage the fire, to charge and discharge the retorter, to remove the lime or other substance used for purification, and to remove that while his done ie office, also to empty the tar reservoir, &c. In the other apparatus, when the oil reservoir is filled and once set to work, it requires an other attendance for a number of hours, then the keeping of the fire in order, and the production of gas can be contained at pleasure, stopped by the mere turning of a cock, and the manances accompanying the formation and removal of tur, ammonical liquor, and lime relics, are entirely modeled.
